You are checking the novelty of a candidate simulation-study design for a judgement-and-decision-making paper. Find the closest existing modelling papers and say whether the specific test has already been done.

CANDIDATE B. WISDOM OF CROWDS UNDER SOCIAL INFLUENCE — OUT-OF-SAMPLE CROSS-DATASET TEST. Fit an individual-level revision model (weight on social information depending on distance and direction, as in Jayles et al. 2017 PNAS 10.1073/pnas.1703695114 and Kao et al. 2018 J R Soc Interface 10.1098/rsif.2018.0130; plus Becker et al. 2017 PNAS 10.1073/pnas.1615978114 revision-accuracy correlation) on one dataset, then predict with fixed parameters the change in crowd error per question in other datasets (Lorenz et al. 2011, Becker 2017/2019, Almaatouq et al. 2020 PNAS). Question: has a single fitted model been tested out-of-sample across pooled continuous-estimation social-influence datasets? Note any integrative/meta-analytic pooled analyses of these experiments (e.g., by Becker, Almaatouq, Jayles, Theraulaz, Tump, Kurvers, Madirolas & de Polavieja, Gürçay et al.).

TOOLS. A Python helper exists at /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_novelty_oa.py (do not edit it; if you need your own script name it /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_novelty_B_*.py). Load keys first in every Bash call: `cd /tmp/jdmsim && set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a; python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py ...`. Commands:
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py cites <W-id>[,<W-id>...] "<search terms or empty>" [abs]` lists works citing any of the IDs (first 50), optional abstracts.
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py search "<terms>" [abs]` full-text search.
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py work <DOI> [<DOI>...]` prints OpenAlex id, year, DOI, title, abstract.
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py ids <DOI>...` resolves OpenAlex IDs.
Known IDs: Jayles 2017 W2767218117; Kao 2018 W2796234406; Becker 2017 W2625771436; Becker 2022 Management Science (10.1287/mnsc.2021.4127) W3157126661. Resolve others (Lorenz 2011 PNAS 10.1073/pnas.1008636108, Almaatouq 2020 PNAS) with `ids`.
Search citing works of Kao 2018, Jayles 2017, Becker 2022, Becker 2017 with terms like "model", "out-of-sample", "pooled", "meta-analysis", "datasets", "revision", "predict", "reanalysis". Also use WebSearch (load with ToolSearch "select:WebSearch,WebFetch") for things like "reanalysis of wisdom of crowds social influence experiments multiple datasets", "social influence wisdom of crowds meta-analysis", Tump/Kurvers "cross-dataset". Read abstracts of the closest hits; read full text (WebFetch) only where needed to decide. Do not download data files. Keep DOIs exactly as returned by OpenAlex/Crossref, never from memory.

Return (compact markdown): (1) closest 3–6 modelling papers with DOI, year, one line on what they did (esp. whether they fitted a revision model on one dataset and predicted others, or pooled several datasets); (2) verdict: NOVEL / PARTLY DONE (say what remains) / DONE; (3) confidence in the verdict (low/medium/high) with one-line reason.

# About me

I am Lukas, a social psychologist, meta-scientist and open science advocate, who mostly uses you to get research done and build the tooling that supports it (in addition to teaching support). I have a solid understanding of software development and infrastructure, but am no expert, so that I will often need clear recommendations and explanations. Most of what I build is tooling for one-off projects, most is not intended to be production-ready or backwards-compatible. Feel free to clarify that project-by-project, but generally lean, efficient and clear code is more important than any backwards-compatible shim or edge-case handling.

I also regularly need your help in writing. For that, and in code, the most annoying failure mode is when history leaks in - when a text argues against its previous versions, or code comments are more about what is gone than about what the curent code does. Here, writing and reviewing outputs from the perspective of a new reader is essential.

# How to work

## Delegation: Fable as Orchestrator

When the session model is Fable, work **orchestrator-first**: plan, delegate substantive work to cheaper subagents, then review and synthesize. Fable itself keeps task decomposition, design decisions and judgment calls, reviewing subagent output, final synthesis and user-facing writing, plus edits so trivial that delegating would take longer. Everything else — implementation, broad searches, analyses, mechanical batch work — goes to subagents by default.

## Using sub-agents

- **Default subagent model: Opus** (`model: "opus"` on the Agent tool / workflow `agent()` calls). Drop to Sonnet or Haiku for clearly mechanical, high-volume steps; reserve Fable-model subagents for only the hardest verify/judge stages.
- **codex CLI** — via the `codex-delegate` skill: (a) independent second opinions and code review (read-only), and (b) self-contained implementation tasks with `--approve-for-me` — good for parallel, independent work streams.
- **agy CLI** (Antigravity; Gemini 3.x + others, `agy models` lists them) — via the `agy-delegate` skill: (a) **large-context reads** — digesting big files, PDFs, logs, or datasets that would bloat Claude context — and (b) **cross-model second opinions**.
- **In Workflow scripts**, reach codex/agy through cheap relay agents: `agent(relayPrompt, {model: 'sonnet', effort: 'low'})`, where `relayPrompt` says "You are a relay agent. Pass the following payload prompt through the `codex-delegate` [or `agy-delegate`] skill, wait for its answer, and return its answer verbatim as your final message; do not answer the payload yourself." followed by the payload, the working directory, and mode/model choices. The relay is pure transport — the skill holds the CLI recipe; keep payload prompts self-contained. Make sure the agents run the request in the foreground, with generous timeout as a subagent that backgrounds codex and waits on monitors/notifications often never gets resumed, stranding the finished answer on disk. If a codex-relay subagent goes quiet, don't wait for it — `ls` for the output file and read it directly.
- Delegation must not degrade quality: give subagents complete, self-contained prompts with all needed context and file paths, and verify load-bearing results yourself rather than trusting a subagent's summary.
- Assign clear ownership of every delegated write target. When two or more agents or processes may write the same file, branch, key, or state object at the same time, give each an independent write target. Different fields in one state file are still one shared target. Merge outputs only when reading or reporting them. If one shared target is required, use one writer, a lock, or sequential phases. Scratch files count as write targets: parallel subagents share one scratchpad directory, so tell each to name its temporary scripts and data after its own task (`scratch_refs_3.py`, not `scratch_build.py`) — otherwise one agent overwrites and executes another's file mid-run.

## Build the Small Tool

When work includes repeated edits, data processing, an analysis, a migration, or a non-trivial check, build the smallest tool that does or verifies it. Use a script, query, generator, codemod, or skill as appropriate. The tool is a reviewable artifact that someone can read and rerun.

Work through one unit to establish the recipe. Build the tool. Run it on that unit and compare its result with the hand-produced result.

Use one deterministic pass when it can handle all units. Delegate building or reviewing that tool when needed; do not assign agents to hand-apply each unit. For delegated work, put the recipe, verification steps, and files agents must not edit in one skill outside their write scope.

Commit the tool when future work will need it.

## Codex CLI (second-opinion / review)

When invoking `codex` non-interactively (e.g. for a second opinion or code review), follow this exact recipe:

1. **Feed the prompt via stdin, with `-` as the prompt arg:**

print the top-level keys before indexing into them.

If a user prompt seems unrelated to the current project/working directory, or references files, concepts, or protocols that don't exist in the codebase, ask the user to confirm before proceeding. They may be in the wrong folder.

Name temporary or throwaway files with a `scratch` prefix (e.g. `scratch.py`, `scratch_notes.md`, `scratch_test.js`). The `/wrap` end-of-session skill detects files matching `scratch*` and offers to commit or delete them during wrap-up.

## Recurring Corrections Become Mechanisms

When the same correction or unexpected failure recurs, encode the fix in a mechanism: a test, hook, lint rule, validation step, safer code default, or automation. Apply the mechanism now and remove the duplicate prose.

Use the strongest mechanism available. Prefer a restriction that makes an invalid state impossible. If that is not possible, use a lint or CI check, a shared helper, or a runtime check.

Keep a prose rule only when it requires judgment. State the decision and the failure mode it prevents.

## Statistical analyses

In my research, I often need your help with statistical analyses. Make sure these are appropriate and robust. If we change direction and another analysis approach becomes more appropriate, we should generally change track (unless compute cost is very high).

### Reproducing / Replicating Prior Analyses

When reproducing, replicating, or re-analysing a previous study, match the original as faithfully as possible by DEFAULT — same sample inclusion rules, same variables, same operationalisations, same model. Do NOT introduce deviations (different year ranges, team/group-size filters, measures, controls, transformations) for convenience, tractability, or unstated preference. If a deviation is genuinely warranted (e.g. to fix a confound, handle censoring, or reduce compute), STOP and flag it explicitly, explain why, and get agreement before building on it. When a deviation is kept, state it and its justification plainly in the writeup and flag it briefly in the code.

# Writing

## Status Reports and Summaries: Plain Over Clever

When reporting progress, findings, or decisions, write like a technical changelog,
not a narrated story. The test: could someone who did not watch the work act on
each sentence without rereading it or asking what it refers to? For that, largely use
ASD-STE100, but deviate where that increases clarity and readability.

Concretely:

1. **Lead with the fact, not the framing.** "Added a manifest hash check at Stage 3
   startup; hashing 300 MB takes 0.10 s" — not "The manifest binding is in,
   positioned with the other startup refusals, and the agent measured the cost
   rather than assuming it."
2. **No process narration.** Skip who suggested what, what was declined, what an
   agent "pushed back" on, and why a fix is "worth noting". Report the decision and
   its one-line reason; drop the story of how it was reached unless asked.
3. **Resolve every reference in place.** Never write "#17", "the #8 question",
   or a label coined earlier in the session without saying what
   it is: "finding #17 (rule-pick caching during outages)". Assume the reader has
   no memory of the earlier conversation.
4. **One clause, one fact.** No sentences that stack a claim, its justification,
   and a contrast with an alternative separated by dashes. Split them.
5. **Structure over prose for multi-item status.** Three or more parallel items
   (fixes applied, decisions pending, open questions) go in a list or short table
   with a bolded label per item, not woven into paragraphs.
6. **Ban editorializing connectors**: "which is the entire point", "worth noting
   because", "the honest answer is", "notably". State the fact; let it carry its
   own weight.
7. **Separate done / pending / needs-my-decision** into visibly distinct blocks,
   so nothing waiting on the user is buried mid-paragraph.

## Jargon: I Know the Concepts, Not the Vocabulary

I have a solid working understanding of programming and systems, but no formal CS
training. Do not dumb things down or pad explanations — just prefer the plain term
when one exists and carries the same meaning: "check before writing" over
"TOCTOU-safe", "lookup table" over "hashmap semantics", "partly overwritten file" 
over "torn write". When a term of art is genuinely the precise word (idempotent, race condition), 
use it, and add a five-word gloss in parentheses the first time it appears in a session if the
meaning isn't clear from context. Never use jargon as compression when a plain
phrase is barely longer.

My written style guides live in `~/Documents/Coding/style_guides`:

- `academic/wallrich_academic_style_guide.md` — voice, spelling, hedging, banned vocabulary, sentence structure, citations, footnotes. Section-specific detail in `academic/sections/{introduction,methods,discussion}.md`. 
- `teaching/wallrich_teaching_style_guide.md` — slides, workshops, handouts, and other audience-facing material.

Read the relevant guide before drafting, revising, or reviewing my prose in that register, and before proposing additions to it.

## Statistical Results in Quarto/Rmd Reports

CRITICAL: NEVER write interpretive prose about statistical results you haven't seen. Produce the numbers first, read the rendered output, then write the text. The full conventions are in the `quarto-reporting` skill. Load it when creating or editing `.qmd` or `.Rmd` files.

## Academic References and DOIs

CRITICAL: NEVER fabricate DOIs, citation metadata, or reference details from memory. DOIs, author lists, titles, page numbers, and volume/issue numbers are exact identifiers — getting them wrong is worse than omitting them.

When creating references:
1. **Always look up DOIs** via the Crossref API (`https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic={url_encoded_reference}`) or web search. Never guess a DOI.
2. **Verify each DOI resolves** by fetching `https://api.crossref.org/works/{DOI}` and checking the returned metadata matches.
3. If a DOI cannot be found, **omit the DOI field** rather than inventing one.
4. For author names, titles, and publication details: verify against Crossref metadata or the publisher's website. Do not rely on memory for these details.

## Reading Academic Articles from HTML

When reading an academic article from an HTML page, ensure the page has fully loaded before extracting or searching its text, and confirm you are actually looking at the full text rather than just the abstract/landing view. A search that comes back empty can mean the content hasn't rendered yet, not that it isn't there. Take a screenshot to see what is actually on the page, before concluding a section is missing or treating the abstract as the whole article.

## Key failure mode - insufficient editing / drift

### The text has no memory of its drafts

Readers see only the final text, never its revision history. They do not know what an earlier draft said, what was wrong with it, or why a claim was softened or dropped. All external writing must read as a clean, self-contained statement of the *current* message, not as a reply to a previous version. Watch for "history leakage": phrasing that only makes sense against a framing the reader never saw. Tells include "not simply X", "rather than Y", "this is not the wrong variable", "to be fair", "the honest limits are narrower", "less a reprieve than a reminder", "we no longer…", and defensive hedges that rebut objections raised only in our own discussion. State the positive claim directly — say what the thing IS and what genuinely limits it, not what it is not relative to a draft.

This applies with full force to durable reference text: CLAUDE.md rules, code comments, docs, commit messages, skill files. A rule states the current fact ("GNU coreutils is on PATH"), never the story of its own correction — no "installed Jul 2026", "exists now", "no longer missing", "fixed since", "never assume X is absent". Those phrasings only make sense to someone who held the old, wrong belief; every future reader starts from the rule itself. Before saving any rule or comment, reread it as a stranger: if it reads as a rebuttal, rewrite it as the fact.

### When we agree to restructure, actually restart

If you and I agree to write a *fresh* draft or a new outline rather than edit the existing one, write it fresh from the agreed outline. Do not silently carry over the previous version's spine, ordering, emphasis, or lead just because it's already there — that is how an obsolete framing survives a "rewrite." Carry over only the verified facts, numbers and sources; treat the prior draft's structure as superseded unless we explicitly decide to keep a part of it.

## API Cost Management

CRITICAL: Before launching any substantial paid-API job (batch LLM calls, large embedding/generation runs, anything looping over many items), explicitly estimate and confirm the cost with me *before* spending:
1. **State the estimate up front**: (price per token × tokens/call × number of calls), and say it out loud before running. Get confirmation for anything beyond a few dollars.
2. **Watch reasoning/thinking models**: a thinking model bills its hidden reasoning tokens as output and can cost ~10-30× a plain model for the same task. Prefer non-thinking models when output is short (e.g. a small JSON), and cap/lower the reasoning budget when a thinking model is needed.

Use `flex` tiers with OpenAi and Gemini that offer batch pricing at the cost of higher latency.
4. **Capture actual spend**: request usage/cost in the response and report it, so estimates can be checked against reality. If a run is substantially more expensive than estimated, stop and re-confirm.

# Coding practices

## Backward Compatibility and Tests

Only add backward-compatibility shims, fallbacks, or dual-format handling in production systems. During development, keep the code clean — delete the old format and move on. If unsure whether something needs backward compatibility, ask before adding it.

Ensure core functionality is covered by tests, but avoid slop and large sets of smoke tests. Less is more.

## Make Reruns Safe

For every command, lifecycle step, or processing loop that may be retried, restarted, or interrupted, design it to reach the correct end state after any number of runs. This includes file-writing scripts and batched external calls.

Check two cases: a second run after success, and a run after interruption at each step. If a prior run may have left partial or stale state, inspect it before continuing. Reuse completed work, repair incomplete outputs, and remove artifacts or locks only after confirming that they are stale.

When deciding whether work is complete, compare stable content or identifiers, not file count or creation order.

## Commands For Me To Run: Copy-Pasteable, Never Illustrative

Any command written for me to run should work as-is when pasted into my shell from the
project root. No placeholders I have to resolve, and no interpreter or tool that is
not on my PATH — I copy what you write and run it.

In practice this means naming the project's own interpreter or entry point rather than
a generic one: `.venv/bin/python -m extract.export --release abc123`, not
`python -m extract.export ...`.

## Verification Before Finishing

Always verify that changes work (run tests, render outputs, check results) before presenting them as complete. Don't leave the user with "to verify, do X" — do it yourself.

When modifying code that produces visual output (plots, charts, UI components), always render and visually inspect the result before presenting the change as complete. Never declare formatting fixes "done" based on code logic alone, except for internal-facing HTML pages. For these, trust your judgement.

When editing something that is deployed (e.g. a GH page), deploying it is part of the task. When the edit is trivial, deploy. When it needs my review, ask for confirmation - but never let me guess whether the latest update is live.

# Working with git

## Committing: Fetch Before Building a Commit Stack

`git fetch` and check `main...origin/main` BEFORE committing, especially when building a stack. 
Also check `git log` for local commits that appeared since the session started (a collaborator or another session may have committed from the same checkout); verify shared files weren't clobbered before stacking on top.

## Parallel Agents in Git Worktrees

- **Merge by the agent's merge-base, never against current main/master.** An agent branches from
  the state that existed when it started, so `git diff main <branch>` carries *deletions of
  everything merged since*; applying it silently reverts already-merged work, with nothing in the
  output to indicate it. Use
  `git diff $(git merge-base main <branch>) <branch> -- <file>` to get only the agent's own
  changes, and re-verify previously merged work after each merge — not just the piece just landed.
- **Remove each worktree as it lands, not at the end.** Each is a full checkout; a wide wave can
  fill the disk mid-session, and worktree creation then fails with "No space left on device".

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. While bypass permissions mode is active:

You can do much of your work through the Bash tool when it is the simpler route: read files with cat, head, or sed -n, search with grep and find, and make small, mechanical file changes with sed, heredocs, or short scripts instead of the dedicated Read, Edit, or Write tools.    ABS: Social information use is widespread in the animal kingdom, helping individuals rapidly acquire useful knowledge and adjust to novel circumstances. In humans, the highly interconnected world provides ample opportunities to benefit from social information but also requires navigating complex social environments with people holding disparate or conflicting views. It is, however, still largely unclear how people integrate information from multiple social sources that (dis)agree with them, and among each other. We address this issue in three steps. First, we present a judgement task in which participants could adjust their judgements after observing the judgements of three peers. We experimentally varied the distribution of this social information, systematically manipulating its variance (extent of agreement among peers) and its skewness (peer judgements clustering either near or far from the participant's judgement). As expected, higher variance among peers reduced their impact on behaviour. Importantly, observing a single peer confirming a participant's own judgement markedly decreased the influence of other-more distant-peers. Second, we develop a framework for modelling the cognitive processes underlying the integration of disparate social information, combining Bayesian updating with simple heuristics. Our model accurately accounts for observed adjustment strategies and reveals that people particularly heed social information that confirms personal judgements. Moreover, the model exposes strong inter-individual differences in strategy use. Third, using simulations, we explore the possible implications of the observed strategies for belief updating. These simulations show how confirmation-based weighting can hamper the influence of disparate social information, exacerbate filter bubble effects and deepen group polarization. Overall, our results clarify what aspects of the social environment are, and are not, conducive to changing people's minds.

# Analysis of Experimental Datasets and Modeling Approach

## (1) Experimental Datasets Reanalyzed

Four published human-subject laboratory experiments were reanalyzed:

"a total of 2885 human participants, organized into 99 independent groups, completed a total of 54 estimation tasks, generating a total of 15,562 individual estimations and 687 collective estimations"

The studies came from prior publications (references 9, 10, 14, 16) involving tasks like "visual estimation, trivia questions, political facts, and economic forecasts."

## (2) Model of Individual Revision

The research uses a weighted averaging framework rather than an explicit individual revision model:

"the collective estimate of the group of agents can be expressed as a convex combination (weighted average) of the initial estimates"

The approach models pre-interaction collective estimates as fully decentralized (ω=0) and post-interaction estimates as potentially centralized (ω>0), without specifying individual-level revision mechanisms.

## (3) Parameter Estimation

Model parameters are **not estimated from data**. Instead, the researchers use an empirical measure called *R* (relative log likelihood of log-normal versus normal distribution fit) as a descriptor of initial-estimate distributions. This measure is "derived empirically" per task and applied uniformly across datasets.

## (4) Out-of-Sample Prediction

**No out-of-sample prediction** is conducted. The analysis uses mixed-effects models with random effects by group and study but does not perform cross-dataset or cross-question validation.

## (5) What Is Predicted

The research predicts the **sign and magnitude of collective error change** based on the interaction between centralization level (ω) and distribution heavy-tailedness (*R*):

"when R<0.5, the error of the revised collective estimate is lower in decentralized influence structures; whereas when R>0.5, the error of the revised collective estimate is lower in centralized structures"

https://openalex.org/W3162309452 2020 https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/ahr7y Towards Stable Principles of Collective Intelligence under an Environment-Dependent Framework cit= 7
   ABS: A large body of work has shown that a group of individuals can often achieve higher levels of intelligence than the group members working alone. Despite these expectations of group advantage, many examples of collective failure have been documented—from market crashes to the spread of false and harmful rumors. To reconcile these results, a major effort in the study of collective decision making has been focused on understanding the role of group composition and communication patterns in promoting the "wisdom of the crowd" or, conversely, leading to "madness of the mob." In the past decades, much of this effort has been devoted to inferring the importance of a particular attribute, in isolation, by its capacity to explain the accuracy of collective judgments. In this thesis, we argue that such a perspective can lead to inconsistent conclusions: an `incoherency problem.' We assert that the importance of an individual-level or structural attribute may change as a function of the environment in which the group is situated. Hence, we propose a research agenda to investigate the relative importance of the group composition and the structure of interaction networks under an environment-dependent framework. We show that under such a framework, we can reconcile previously conflicting claims from the collective intelligence literature and motivate a future research program to identify stable principles of collective performance. Although implementing such a program is logistically challenging, "virtual lab" experiments of the sort discussed in this thesis, in combination with emerging "open science" practices such as pre-registration, data availability, open code, and "many-labs" collaborations, offer a promising route forward.
https://openalex.org/W7204128569 2026 https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04499 Leveraging Collective Advice-Taking Behavior to Infer Accuracy and Improve the Wisdom of Crowds cit= 0
   ABS: Wisdom of crowds estimates can be compromised when some agents’ predictions are systematically biased. A natural remedy is to aggregate predictions from a subset of more accurate agents rather than the entire crowd. I propose cluster weight on advice (CWOA), a novel “two-shot” algorithm to identify a more accurate subgroup in a single-prediction-problem context. CWOA first applies kernel density estimation to identify clusters of similar initial predictions. If multiple clusters emerge—indicating potential heterogeneity in agents’ information—the algorithm proceeds to present a piece of numerical advice (e.g., the group mean) and elicit updated predictions. This enables the calculation of the weight on advice (WOA)—the scaled magnitude of each agent’s belief revision. CWOA then averages the updated predictions within the cluster with the lowest mean WOA. A behavioral model and simulations explain both why and when cluster-level WOA signals accuracy. Better-informed agents—having already incorporated higher-quality information—perceive less corrective value in the advice and therefore, exhibit lower WOA. CWOA does not require agents to know the true biases or the composition of the crowd; a modest relative advantage in perceived estimation bias by better-informed agents may be sufficient, even under misperceptions of variance, advice quality, and psychological biases in advice taking. Empirically, I first test and confirm the model’s key insight in a controlled experimental setting. I then validate CWOA’s performance across multiple preregistered and archival data sets, including a study in which numerical advice comes from artificial intelligence. CWOA consistently outperforms benchmarks, including the state-of-the-art metaprediction-based methods. This paper was accepted by Jack Soll, behavioral economics and decision analysis. https://openalex.org/W1906769221 2015 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0140406 Opinion Formation by Social Influence: From Experiments to Modeling cit= 60
   ABS: Predicting different forms of collective behavior in human populations, as the outcome of individual attitudes and their mutual influence, is a question of major interest in social sciences. In particular, processes of opinion formation have been theoretically modeled on the basis of a formal similarity with the dynamics of certain physical systems, giving rise to an extensive collection of mathematical models amenable to numerical simulation or even to exact solution. Empirical ground for these models is however largely missing, which confine them to the level of mere metaphors of the real phenomena they aim at explaining. In this paper we present results of an experiment which quantifies the change in the opinions given by a subject on a set of specific matters under the influence of others. The setup is a variant of a recently proposed experiment, where the subject's confidence on his or her opinion was evaluated as well. In our realization, which records the quantitative answers of 85 subjects to 20 questions before and after an influence event, the focus is put on characterizing the change in answers and confidence induced by such influence. Similarities and differences with the previous version of the experiment are highlighted. We find that confidence changes are to a large extent independent of any other recorded quantity, while opinion changes are strongly modulated by the original confidence. On the other hand, opinion changes are not influenced by the initial difference with the reference opinion. The typical time scales on which opinion varies are moreover substantially longer than those of confidence change. Experimental results are then used to estimate parameters for a dynamical agent-based model of opinion formation in a large population. In the context of the model, we study the convergence to full consensus and the effect of opinion leaders on the collective distribution of opinions.
https://openalex.org/W3193304031 2021 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2106292118 Dynamical system model predicts when social learners impair collective performance cit= 32
   ABS: A key question concerning collective decisions is whether a social system can settle on the best available option when some members learn from others instead of evaluating the options on their own. This question is challenging to study, and previous research has reached mixed conclusions, because collective decision outcomes depend on the insufficiently understood complex system of cognitive strategies, task properties, and social influence processes. In particular, it investigates how the interplay of the proportion of social learners, the relative merit of options, and the type of conformity response affect collective decision outcomes in a binary choice. The model predicts that, when the proportion of social learners exceeds a critical threshold, a bistable state appears in which the majority can end up favoring either the higher- or lower-merit option, depending on fluctuations and initial conditions. Below this threshold, the high-merit option is chosen by the majority. The critical threshold is determined by the conformity response function and the relative merits of the two options. The study helps reconcile disagreements about the effect of social learners on collective performance and proposes a mathematical framework that can be readily adapted to extensions investigating a wider variety of dynamics.
https://openalex.org/W3214901083 2021 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009590 Crowd control: Reducing individual estimation bias by sharing biased social information cit= 6
   ABS: Cognitive biases are widespread in humans and animals alike, and can sometimes be reinforced by social interactions. One prime bias in judgment and decision-making is the human tendency to underestimate large quantities. Previous research on social influence in estimation tasks has generally focused on the impact of single estimates on individual and collective accuracy, showing that randomly sharing estimates does not reduce the underestimation bias. Here, we test a method of social information sharing that exploits the known relationship between the true value and the level of underestimation, and study if it can counteract the underestimation bias. We performed estimation experiments in which participants had to estimate a series of quantities twice, before and after receiving estimates from one or several group members. Our purpose was threefold: to study (i) whether restructuring the sharing of social information can reduce the underestimation bias, (ii) how the number of estimates received affects the sensitivity to social influence and estimation accuracy, and (iii) the mechanisms underlying the integration of multiple estimates. Our restructuring of social interactions successfully countered the underestimation bias. Moreover, we find that sharing more than one estimate also reduces the underestimation bias. Underlying our results are a human tendency to herd, to trust larger estimates than one's own more than smaller estimates, and to follow disparate social information less. Using a computational modeling approach, we demonstrate that these effects are indeed key to explain the experimental results. Overall, our results show that existing knowledge on biases can be used to dampen their negative effects and boost judgment accuracy, paving the way for combating other cognitive biases threatening collective systems.
https://openalex.org/W3168407451 2021 https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2021.0231 Impact of sharing full versus averaged social information on social influence and estimation accuracy cit= 9
   ABS: The recent developments of social networks and recommender systems have dramatically increased the amount of social information shared in human communities, challenging the human ability to process it. Here, we compare the performance of groups in estimation tasks when social information is fully shared versus when it is first averaged and then shared. We find that improvements in estimation accuracy are comparable in both cases. However, our results reveal important differences in subjects' behaviour: (i) subjects follow the social information more when receiving an average than when receiving all estimates, and this effect increases with the number of estimates underlying the average; (ii) subjects follow the social information more when it is higher than their personal estimate than when it is lower. This effect is stronger when receiving all estimates than when receiving an average. We introduce a model that sheds light on these effects, and confirms their importance for explaining improvements in estimation accuracy in all treatments.
https://openalex.org/W3084405331 2020 https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2020.0496 The impact of incorrect social information on collective wisdom in human groups cit= 24
   ABS: A major problem resulting from the massive use of social media is the potential spread of incorrect information. Yet, very few studies have investigated the impact of incorrect information on individual and collective decisions. We performed experiments in which participants had to estimate a series of quantities, before and after receiving social information. Unbeknownst to them, we controlled the degree of inaccuracy of the social information through 'virtual influencers', who provided some incorrect information. We find that a large proportion of individuals only partially follow the social information, thus resisting incorrect information. Moreover, incorrect information can help improve group performance more than correct information, when going against a human underestimation bias. We then design a computational model whose predictions are in good agreement with the empirical data, and sheds light on the mechanisms underlying our results. Besides these main findings, we demonstrate that the dispersion of estimates varies a lot between quantities, and must thus be considered when normalizing and aggregating estimates of quantities that are very different in nature. Overall, our results suggest that incorrect information does not necessarily impair the collective wisdom of groups, and can even be used to dampen the negative effects of known cognitive biases.
https://openalex.org/W4385309125 2023 https://doi.org/10.1137/22m1492751 How Social Influence Affects the Wisdom of Crowds in Influence Networks cit= 7
   ABS: Abstract. A long-standing debate is whether social influence improves the collective wisdom of a crowd or undermines it. This paper addresses the question based on a naïve learning setting in influence systems theory: in our models individuals evolve their estimates of an unknown truth according to the weighted-average opinion dynamics. A formal mathematization is provided with rigorous theoretical analysis. We obtain various conditions for improving, optimizing, and undermining the crowd accuracy, respectively. We prove that if the wisdom of a finite-size group is improved, then the collective estimate converges to the truth as the group size increases. We show that whether social influence improves or undermines the wisdom is determined by the social power allocations in the influence system: if the influence system allocates relatively larger social power to relatively more accurate individuals, it improves the wisdom; on the contrary, if the influence system assigns less social power to more accurate individuals, it undermines the wisdom. At a population level, individuals’ susceptibilities to interpersonal influence and network centralities are both crucial. To improve the wisdom, more accurate individuals should be less susceptible and have larger network centralities. Particularly, in democratic influence networks, if relatively more accurate individuals are relatively less susceptible, the wisdom is improved; if more accurate individuals are more susceptible, the wisdom is undermined, which is consistent with the reported empirical evidence. Our investigation provides a theoretical framework for understanding the role social influence plays in the emergence of collective wisdom.

No published paper I found fits an individual-level revision model on one continuous-estimation social-influence dataset and then predicts, with fixed parameters, the change in crowd error per question in other datasets. Pooled reanalyses exist, but they either fit nothing at the individual level or stay within one dataset or one lab.

## (1) Closest existing work

| Paper | DOI | What it did |
|---|---|---|
| **Almaatouq, Rahimian, Burton & Alhajri 2022, Sci Rep** (preprint 2020, [arXiv 2006.12471](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.12471)) | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-20551-7 | Pooled reanalysis of four datasets: Lorenz 2011, Becker 2017, Gürçay 2015 and Becker 2019 (2,885 participants, 54 tasks). The model treats the crowd estimate as a weighted average of initial estimates, with a centralisation parameter. It uses a descriptor of the initial-estimate distribution (R) to predict when centralised influence lowers crowd error. Per a fetched summary of the paper, it fits no individual-level revision parameters, uses mixed-effects models with study as a random effect, and makes no cross-dataset prediction. |
| **Madirolas & de Polavieja 2015, PLoS Comput Biol** | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1004594 | Builds a revision model (weighted geometric mean of own and social estimate). It is tested on the Lorenz 2011 data only. Social weight w_s = 0.68 is estimated in one condition and used to predict another condition of the same experiment. |
| **Jayles et al. 2017 PNAS; Jayles et al. 2020 J R Soc Interface; Jayles et al. 2021 J R Soc Interface; Jayles et al. 2021 PLoS Comput Biol** | https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1703695114 ; https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2020.0496 ; https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2021.0231 ; https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009590 | A revision model with distance- and direction-dependent social weight, refit within each new experiment of the same lab and paradigm. It reproduces collective accuracy within those experiments. It is not tested on other labs' datasets. |
| **Kao et al. 2018, J R Soc Interface** | https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2018.0130 | Fits a social-weight revision model that depends on distance and direction, on the authors' own experiment. I did not read the full text, so I have not confirmed whether it applies the model to external datasets. |
| **Molleman et al. 2020, Proc R Soc B** | https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2020.2413 | Fits a cognitive model of how people combine several disagreeing peer estimates, on one new experiment. The model is not applied to other datasets. |
| **Becker, Almaatouq et al. 2020, arXiv "Network structures of collective intelligence: the contingent benefits of group discussion"** | https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2009.07202 | Applies a network belief-formation framework across discussion versus Delphi-style formats, from the abstract only. It uses no fitted individual revision model and makes no out-of-sample prediction. |

Other checks:
- **Almaatouq's thesis** (https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/ahr7y) and **Almaatouq et al., "Beyond playing 20 questions with nature"** (https://doi.org/10.1017/s0140525x22002874) call for integrative, cross-environment tests. They do not carry them out for this model.
- **Chacoma & Zanette 2015** (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0140406) estimates model parameters from a single experiment.
- **Lin 2026, Management Science** (https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04499) validates a weight-on-advice aggregation algorithm across several archival datasets. It does not predict change in crowd error from a fitted revision model.
- Searches for meta-analyses or pooled analyses by the Tump/Kurvers or Theraulaz groups found nothing that fits a model across datasets.

## (2) Verdict: PARTLY DONE

- **Already done:**
  - Pooling several of the target datasets to explain the sign of crowd-error change (Almaatouq et al. 2022).
  - Checking a revision model on a dataset collected by someone else, but only within Lorenz 2011 and only at the individual level (Madirolas & de Polavieja 2015).
  - Refitting the Jayles-type revision model across experiments from one lab.
- **Still open:**
  - One fixed-parameter revision model fitted on dataset A, with weights that depend on distance and direction plus a link between accuracy and amount of revision.
  - Used to predict the per-question change in crowd error across datasets from other labs (Lorenz 2011, Becker 2017/2019, Almaatouq 2020, Jayles/Kao).
  - Scored against those observed changes.
  - Compared with the per-dataset R-descriptor account in Almaatouq et al. 2022.

## (3) Confidence: medium

- **Why:** Coverage of work citing Jayles 2017, Kao 2018, Becker 2017, Lorenz 2011, Almaatouq 2022 and Madirolas 2015 in OpenAlex, plus web searches, turned up only the pooled analysis without a fitted model.
- **Not fully checked:** The supplementary material of Becker 2017, Kao 2018 and Almaatouq 2022, which I did not read. An unpublished thesis or 2025–26 preprint could also have done this.
